\chapter{Taking, Asking, Helping — and the Backwards Verb}
\label{ch:spanish-backwards-verb}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I take, ask and help in Spanish, and build a sentence with gustar the way Spanish actually builds it — with the thing liked as the subject.}

Say tomar, preguntar and ayudar, then turn gustar around: me gusta el libro is the book pleasing me, so the verb agrees with the thing and the person moves into the little word in front.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tomar]{tomar — \textquotedblleft{}to take\textquotedblright{}, and nobody knows where it came from}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-tomar}



\begin{quote}
Every verb so far ran straight back to a Latin root you could name. Here is one that does not — and the gap is the useful part.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one soft tap of the tongue: \emph{to-MAR}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-o} — a short, pure \emph{o}, with no English glide toward \emph{ow}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tomar} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to take}\textquotedblright{}) is a plain \emph{-ar} verb: \textbf{tomo, tomas, toma, tomamos, toman}. It is one of the most common verbs in the language, and its origin is \textbf{genuinely unsettled}.

The leading proposal derives it from Latin \emph{autumāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to take as, to assert\textquotedblright{}, worn down through an intermediate \emph{tumar}; a rival one points to a pre-Roman Iberian word Latin never recorded. Neither is proved, and careful dictionaries say so. \textquotedblleft{}We don't know\textquotedblright{} is a real answer in etymology.

It carries a second everyday sense across Latin America: \textbf{to drink}. A waiter asking \emph{¿Qué vas a tomar?} is asking what you would like.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Latin's own \textquotedblleft{}gather up\textquotedblright{} verb survived perfectly well: \textbf{coger} $\leftarrow$ \textbf{colligere}, which is \emph{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{legere} — the very root you met in \emph{leer}. English took that same Latin word twice: \textbf{collect} straight from the Latin, and \textbf{coil} by way of French.

In Spain \emph{coger} is the plain everyday word: \emph{coger el autobús}, catch the bus. In much of Latin America — Argentina, Mexico and well beyond — it is \textbf{coarse slang for sex}, and using it innocently will derail a conversation. \emph{Tomar} is safe on both sides of the Atlantic, which is a large part of why it won.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tomo, tomas, toma, tomamos, toman\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tomo un café\textquotedblright{} — I'll have a coffee
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tomo el autobús\textquotedblright{} — the safe way to say it anywhere
  \item \textquotedblleft{}coger\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}collect, coil\textquotedblright{} — one root, and one place to be careful
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \emph{tomar} have a confirmed etymology? (\textbf{No} — \emph{autumāre} and a pre-Roman source are both unproved.) What Latin verb gives \emph{coger}, and which root sits inside it? (\emph{Colligere}, holding \emph{legere}, \textquotedblleft{}to gather\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{leer}.) Why reach for \emph{tomar} instead? (\emph{Coger} is coarse slang across much of Latin America.) Next: \textbf{preguntar}, and the two different asks.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[preguntar]{preguntar — \textquotedblleft{}to ask\textquotedblright{}, by sounding the water with a pole}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-preguntar}



\begin{quote}
English gets by with one verb, \emph{ask}. Spanish splits the job in two, and picking the wrong half is a reliable beginner mistake. Here is the first half.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{pr-cluster} — \emph{pre-} is one crisp beat, \emph{preh}, with a tapped \emph{r}.
  \item \texttt{g-hard} — the \emph{g} before \emph{u} is hard, as in English \emph{gun}: \emph{pre-goon-TAR}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{preguntar} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to ask a question}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Vulgar Latin \textbf{praecunctāre}, itself a reshaping of classical \textbf{percontārī}, \textquotedblleft{}to inquire\textquotedblright{}. And \emph{percontārī} was built on \textbf{contus}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a punting pole}\textquotedblright{}: to \emph{percontor} was to push a pole down through water and find out how deep it was.

Asking is taking a sounding. Unlike almost every other word here, \emph{preguntar} left English nothing — the pole word died out — yet English rebuilt the same metaphor on its own: you \emph{sound someone out}, you \emph{probe}.

The verb is a plain \emph{-ar} one: \textbf{pregunto, preguntas, pregunta, preguntamos, preguntan}. Its noun is \textbf{la pregunta} (fem.), and note that Spanish \emph{makes} a question rather than asking one: \emph{hacer una pregunta}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one English \textquotedblleft{}ask\textquotedblright{}, two Spanish verbs}]
Spanish sorts asking by \textbf{what you are after}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you want} & \textbf{verb} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
information & \textbf{preguntar} & \emph{Te pregunto la hora} — I'm asking you the time \\
a thing or a favour & \textbf{pedir} & \emph{Pido un café} — I'm asking for a coffee \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Ask for a coffee with \emph{preguntar} and you have said \textquotedblleft{}I question a coffee\textquotedblright{}. The line is simple: a question takes \emph{preguntar}, a request takes \emph{pedir}.

\textbf{pedir} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{petere}, \textquotedblleft{}to make for, to aim at\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{that} root stocked English generously: \textbf{petition}, \textbf{appetite}, \textbf{compete}, \textbf{impetus}, \textbf{perpetual}, \textbf{centripetal}. It cracks a third way, \emph{e} $\to$ \emph{i}: \textbf{pido, pides, pide, pedimos, piden}. Recognise \emph{pido} for now; the pattern gets its own lesson later.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pregunto, preguntas, pregunta, preguntamos, preguntan\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te pregunto la hora\textquotedblright{} — I'm asking you the time
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Pido un café\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Tomo un café\textquotedblright{} — I ask for one, I have one
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pedir\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}petition, appetite, compete\textquotedblright{} — the aiming family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{percontārī} picture literally? (\textbf{Sounding water with a pole}.) Which verb asks for a coffee, and which asks the time? (\emph{Pedir} for the coffee; \emph{preguntar} for the time.) What Latin root is \emph{pedir} from, and one English cousin? (\emph{Petere}, \textquotedblleft{}to aim at\textquotedblright{} — \emph{petition, appetite, compete}.) Next: \textbf{ayudar}, which is the same word as English \emph{aid}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ayudar]{ayudar — \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{}, and it is English \textquotedblleft{}aid\textquotedblright{} in disguise}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-ayudar}



\begin{quote}
You can ask a question now. The next thing to ask for is a hand — and this verb is one you already own in English without knowing it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — a clean, open \emph{a}: \emph{a-yoo-DAR}.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one tap at the end, not an English \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ayudar} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to help}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{adiūtāre}, the repeating form of \textbf{adiuvāre}: \textbf{ad-} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{iuvāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to help, to delight\textquotedblright{}). To help was to move toward someone.

English borrowed that identical verb through Old French \emph{aidier} and calls it \textbf{aid}. So \emph{ayudar} and \emph{aid} are not merely cousins — they are the \textbf{same word} by two different roads. The family came with it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{aide}, and \textbf{aide-de-camp}, an officer who helps.
  \item \textbf{adjutant} — the officer whose whole job is assisting.
  \item \textbf{adjuvant} — a substance that helps another drug work.
  \item \textbf{coadjutor} — one who helps alongside.
\end{itemize}

The shape change is a rule, not an accident. Latin \textbf{-di-} before a vowel turned into Spanish \textbf{y}: \emph{adiūtāre} $\to$ \textbf{ayudar}, \emph{hodiē} $\to$ \textbf{hoy} (\textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}), \emph{podium} $\to$ \emph{poyo}. Once you have that, the word stops looking arbitrary.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a plain -ar verb, and how to ask for a hand}]
Nothing breaks; the endings are the ones you started with:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{form} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{ayudo} & I help \\
tú & \textbf{ayudas} & you help \\
nosotros & \textbf{ayudamos} & we help \\
ellos/ustedes & \textbf{ayudan} & they help \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Its noun is \textbf{la ayuda} (fem.), \textquotedblleft{}help\textquotedblright{} — the word on relief packages worldwide. Two sentences worth owning: \emph{\textbf{¿Me ayudas?}} (\textquotedblleft{}will you help me?\textquotedblright{} — Spanish uses the plain present where English needs \emph{will}) and, politely, \emph{\textbf{¿Puedo ayudarle?}}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ayudo, ayudas, ayudamos, ayudan\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Me ayudas?\textquotedblright{} — will you help me?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te pregunto\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Me ayudas\textquotedblright{} — I ask you, you help me
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ayudar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}aid, adjutant, adjuvant\textquotedblright{} — one word, two roads
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin pieces build \emph{adiuvāre}? (\textbf{Ad-} \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{iuvāre} \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{}.) What everyday English word is \emph{ayudar}, arriving by French? (\textbf{Aid}.) What sound-law turned \emph{adiūtāre} into \emph{ayudar}, and which other word shows it? (Latin \textbf{-di-} became Spanish \textbf{y}; \emph{hodiē} $\to$ \emph{hoy}.) Next: \textbf{gustar}, the verb that runs backwards.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gustar]{gustar — the verb that runs backwards}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-gustar}



\begin{quote}
Back in the introductions you learned \textbf{mucho gusto} — \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{}. Here is the verb that noun belongs to, assembled the opposite way round from English. It is the single thing in Spanish that trips English speakers up hardest.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{g-hard} — a hard \emph{g} before \emph{u}: \emph{goos-TAR}.
  \item \texttt{s-clear} — a clean hissing \emph{s}, never a \emph{z} buzz.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gustar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{gustāre}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to taste}\textquotedblright{}. English kept the root and stayed close to the tongue:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{gusto} — doing something with relish, that is, with a taste for it.
  \item \textbf{gustatory} — of the sense of taste.
  \item \textbf{disgust} — \emph{dis-} \textquotedblleft{}away\textquotedblright{} + taste: what you spit back out.
  \item \textbf{degustation}, a tasting menu; and through French, \textbf{ragout}.
\end{itemize}

Spanish's own \textbf{el gusto} — the \emph{gusto} of \emph{mucho gusto} — still holds both senses: taste on the tongue, and pleasure taken in a thing. The verb followed the second: \emph{gustar} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to please}\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the thing you like is the subject}]
English says \textbf{I} like the book: the liker is the subject. Spanish has no such sentence. It says \textbf{Me gusta el libro} — \textquotedblleft{}the book is pleasing \textbf{to me}\textquotedblright{}.

Everything follows from that:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el libro} is the \textbf{subject}, which is why the verb is \emph{gusta}, third person.
  \item \emph{me} is the person it happens \textbf{to}, not the one doing anything.
\end{itemize}

So the verb agrees with the \textbf{thing}, never with you:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you mean} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{why} \\
\midrule
I like the book & \textbf{Me gusta el libro} & one book, so \emph{gusta} \\
I like books & \textbf{Me gustan los libros} & many books, so \emph{gustan} \\
I like reading & \textbf{Me gusta leer} & one action, so \emph{gusta} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

To change who is pleased, change the little word in front, not the verb: \textbf{me} (to me), \textbf{te} (to you), \textbf{le} (to him, her, \emph{usted}), \textbf{nos} (to us), \textbf{les} (to them).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Careful.} There is no \emph{yo gusto el libro}. \emph{Yo gusto} is a real sentence — it means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I} am pleasing\textquotedblright{} — just not the one you were reaching for.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Me gusta el café\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Me gustan los libros\textquotedblright{} — the verb follows the thing
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Te gusta tomar café\textquotedblright{} — you like drinking coffee
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Me gusta ayudar\textquotedblright{} — I like helping
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gustar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}gusto, disgust, gustatory\textquotedblright{} — the tasting family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \emph{me gusta el libro}, what is the subject? (\textbf{El libro}.) Why is it \emph{me gustan los libros}? (The verb agrees with \emph{los libros}, which is plural.) What did \emph{gustāre} mean, and name an English cousin. (\textbf{To taste}; \emph{gusto, disgust}.) And what would \emph{yo gusto} actually mean? (\textbf{I} am pleasing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
